False.elim.comment:
`False.elim : False → C` says that from `False`, any desired proposition
`C` holds. Also known as ex falso quodlibet (EFQ) or the principle of explosion.

The target type is actually `C : Sort u` which means it works for both
propositions and types. When executed, this acts like an "unreachable"
instruction: it is **undefined behavior** to run, but it will probably print
"unreachable code". (You would need to construct a proof of false to run it
anyway, which you can only do using `sorry` or unsound axioms.)
False.elim.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def False.elim {C : Sort u} (h : False) : C :=   h.rec
False.elim.description: From a contradiction, any proposition can be inferred, illustrating that if something is false, anything follows.

Nat.not_lt_zero.description: A natural number cannot be less than zero.

Nonempty.intro.code: Nonempty.intro.{u} {α : Sort u} (val : α) : Nonempty α
Nonempty.intro.description: If there exists an element of a type, then that type is considered nonempty.

HEq.rfl.code: HEq.rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : HEq a a
HEq.rfl.comment: A version of `HEq.refl` with an implicit argument.
HEq.rfl.fullDefinition: @[match_pattern] protected def HEq.rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : HEq a a :=   HEq.refl a
HEq.rfl.description: A special case of equality, where an element is equal to itself, is represented with implicit arguments.

rfl.code: rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
rfl.comment:
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
rfl.fullDefinition: @[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
rfl.description: An element is equal to itself, with an implicit argument allowing for broader applications of this concept.

Eq.symm.code: Eq.symm.{u} {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : a = b) : b = a
Eq.symm.comment:
Equality is symmetric: if `a = b` then `b = a`.

Because this is in the `Eq` namespace, if you have a variable `h : a = b`,
`h.symm` can be used as shorthand for `Eq.symm h` as a proof of `b = a`.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
Eq.symm.description: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.

Eq.trans.code: Eq.trans.{u} {α : Sort u} {a b c : α} (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : b = c) : a = c
Eq.trans.comment:
Equality is transitive: if `a = b` and `b = c` then `a = c`.

Because this is in the `Eq` namespace, if you have variables or expressions
`h₁ : a = b` and `h₂ : b = c`, you can use `h₁.trans h₂ : a = c` as shorthand
for `Eq.trans h₁ h₂`.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
Eq.trans.description: If one element is equal to a second, and that second is equal to a third, then the first element is also equal to the third, demonstrating the transitive property of equality.

Or.inl.code: Or.inl {a b : Prop} (h : a) : a ∨ b
Or.inl.comment: `Or.inl` is "left injection" into an `Or`. If `h : a` then `Or.inl h : a ∨ b`.
Or.inl.description: If a proposition is true, then it can be included in a disjunction, demonstrating how to inject it into the logical framework of 'or'.

Or.inr.code: Or.inr {a b : Prop} (h : b) : a ∨ b
Or.inr.comment: `Or.inr` is "right injection" into an `Or`. If `h : b` then `Or.inr h : a ∨ b`.
Or.inr.description: If there is a proof of a proposition, it can be included in a disjunction as the second option.

Bool.true.comment: The boolean value `true`, not to be confused with the proposition `True`.
Bool.true.description: The statement identifies the boolean value representing true, which is distinct from the logical proposition denoting truth.

List.nil.description: The empty list is represented by the notation for an empty collection with no elements.

Bool.false.comment: The boolean value `false`, not to be confused with the proposition `False`.
Bool.false.description: The boolean value false is a specific representation of the false state in boolean logic.

Lean.Syntax.atom.comment:
An `atom` corresponds to a keyword or piece of literal unquoted syntax.
These correspond to quoted strings inside `syntax` declarations.
For example, in `(x + y)`, `"("`, `"+"` and `")"` are `atom`
and `x` and `y` are `ident`.
Lean.Syntax.atom.description: An atom represents a keyword or literal piece of unquoted syntax, corresponding to quoted strings found within syntax declarations.

List.cons.code: List.cons.{u} {α : Type u} (head : α) (tail : List α) : List α
List.cons.comment:
If `a : α` and `l : List α`, then `cons a l`, or `a :: l`, is the
list whose first element is `a` and with `l` as the rest of the list.
List.cons.description: The construction of a list adds a specified element at the beginning, followed by the remaining elements of an existing list.

Eq.refl.code: Eq.refl.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} (a : α) : a = a
Eq.refl.comment:
`Eq.refl a : a = a` is reflexivity, the unique constructor of the
equality type. See also `rfl`, which is usually used instead.
Eq.refl.description: An element is equal to itself, represented by a unique constructor of the equality type.

Membership.mem.code: Membership.mem.{u, v} {α : outParam (Type u)} {γ : Type v} [self : Membership α γ] : α → γ → Prop
Membership.mem.comment: The membership relation `a ∈ s : Prop` where `a : α`, `s : γ`.
Membership.mem.description: The membership relation defines a property indicating that an element belongs to a set.

or.comment:
`or x y`, or `x || y`, is the boolean "or" operation (not to be confused
with `Or : Prop → Prop → Prop`, which is the propositional connective).
It is `@[macro_inline]` because it has C-like short-circuiting behavior:
if `x` is true then `y` is not evaluated.
or.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def or (x y : Bool) : Bool :=   match x with   | true  => true   | false => y
or.description: The boolean "or" operation returns true if at least one of its two operands is true, with short-circuiting behavior so that the second operand is not evaluated if the first is true.

Decidable.isFalse.comment: Prove that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p`
Decidable.isFalse.description: If a proposition is shown to be false, then its negation is decisively established.

Decidable.isTrue.comment: Prove that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p`
Decidable.isTrue.description: If a proposition is proven to be true, then it is decisively established.

id.comment:
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
id.fullDefinition: @[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a
id.description: The identity function returns its input unchanged and can be used to explicitly assign a type to an expression for typeclass inference purposes.

outParam.comment:
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
outParam.fullDefinition: @[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α
outParam.description: This defines a mechanism to create output parameters in type classes, allowing type inference to determine specific types based on other known values.

Lean.TSyntax.mk.description: A syntax node is created from a specified kind and raw syntax input, resulting in a type-safe representation of the syntax.

Inhabited.mk.code: Inhabited.mk.{u} {α : Sort u} (default : α) : Inhabited α
Inhabited.mk.description: Any type that has a default element is considered inhabited.

Function.comp.code: Function.comp.{u, v, w} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {δ : Sort w} (f : β → δ) (g : α → β) : α → δ
Function.comp.comment:
Function composition is the act of pipelining the result of one function, to the input of another, creating an entirely new function.
Example:
```
#eval Function.comp List.reverse (List.drop 2) [3, 2, 4, 1]
-- [1, 4]
```
You can use the notation `f ∘ g` as shorthand for `Function.comp f g`.
```
#eval (List.reverse ∘ List.drop 2) [3, 2, 4, 1]
-- [1, 4]
```
A simpler way of thinking about it, is that `List.reverse ∘ List.drop 2`
is equivalent to `fun xs => List.reverse (List.drop 2 xs)`,
the benefit is that the meaning of composition is obvious,
and the representation is compact.
Function.comp.fullDefinition: @[inline] def Function.comp {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {δ : Sort w} (f : β → δ) (g : α → β) : α → δ :=   fun x => f (g x)
Function.comp.description: Function composition combines two functions into a new function, where the output of the second function becomes the input of the first.

id_eq.code: id_eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} (a : α) : id a = a
id_eq.description: The identity function returns each element unchanged, establishing that applying it to any element results in that same element.

Inhabited.default.code: Inhabited.default.{u} {α : Sort u} [self : Inhabited α] : α
Inhabited.default.comment:
`default` is a function that produces a "default" element of any
`Inhabited` type. This element does not have any particular specified
properties, but it is often an all-zeroes value.
Inhabited.default.description: This defines a function that generates a default element for any inhabited type, which is a type that has at least one value.

Subtype.val.code: Subtype.val.{u} {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop} (self : Subtype p) : α
Subtype.val.comment:
If `s : {x // p x}` then `s.val : α` is the underlying element in the base
type. You can also write this as `s.1`, or simply as `s` when the type is
known from context.
Subtype.val.fullDefinition: val : α   /-- If `s : {x // p x}` then `s.2` or `s.property` is the assertion that   `p s.1`, that is, that `s` is in fact an element for which `p` holds. -/   property : p val
Subtype.val.description: The value of a subtype is the underlying element from the base type that satisfies a given property.

DecidableEq.comment:
Asserts that `α` has decidable equality, that is, `a = b` is decidable
for all `a b : α`. See `Decidable`.
DecidableEq.fullDefinition: abbrev DecidableEq (α : Sort u) :=   (a b : α) → Decidable (Eq a b)
DecidableEq.description: A type is said to have decidable equality if it is possible to determine whether any two elements of that type are equal.

Prod.fst.code: Prod.fst.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (self : α × β) : α
Prod.fst.comment: The first projection out of a pair. if `p : α × β` then `p.1 : α`.
Prod.fst.fullDefinition: fst : α   /-- The second projection out of a pair. if `p : α × β` then `p.2 : β`. -/   snd : β
Prod.fst.description: This defines a function that retrieves the first element from a given pair of values.

Prod.snd.code: Prod.snd.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (self : α × β) : β
Prod.snd.comment: The second projection out of a pair. if `p : α × β` then `p.2 : β`.
Prod.snd.description: This defines a function that retrieves the second element from a given pair of values.

DecidablePred.code: DecidablePred.{u} {α : Sort u} (r : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)
DecidablePred.fullDefinition: abbrev DecidablePred {α : Sort u} (r : α → Prop) :=   (a : α) → Decidable (r a)
DecidablePred.description: A decidable predicate is a property that can be determined to be either true or false for elements of a type.

ite.code: ite.{u} {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α
ite.comment:
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.
ite.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=   h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
ite.description: This defines a function that implements an "if-then-else" conditional structure, returning one of two values based on the truth of a given decidable proposition.

List.foldl.code: List.foldl.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (f : α → β → α) (init : α) : List β → α
List.foldl.comment:
Folds a function over a list from the left:
`foldl f z [a, b, c] = f (f (f z a) b) c`
List.foldl.fullDefinition: def List.foldl {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (f : α → β → α) : (init : α) → List β → α   | a, nil      => a   | a, cons b l => foldl f (f a b) l
List.foldl.description: This defines a function that iteratively applies a binary operation to elements of a list, accumulating a result by processing the list from left to right, starting with an initial value.

List.concat.code: List.concat.{u} {α : Type u} : List α → α → List α
List.concat.comment: `l.concat a` appends `a` at the *end* of `l`, that is, `l ++ [a]`.
List.concat.fullDefinition: def List.concat {α : Type u} : List α → α → List α   | nil,       b => cons b nil   | cons a as, b => cons a (concat as b)
List.concat.description: This defines a function that appends a single element to the end of a list, effectively creating a new list that includes both the original elements and the added element.

List.length.code: List.length.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} : List α → ℕ
List.length.comment:
The length of a list: `[].length = 0` and `(a :: l).length = l.length + 1`.

This function is overridden in the compiler to `lengthTR`, which uses constant
stack space, while leaving this function to use the "naive" recursion which is
easier for reasoning.
List.length.fullDefinition: def List.length : List α → Nat   | nil       => 0   | cons _ as => HAdd.hAdd (length as) 1
List.length.description: This defines a function that computes the number of elements in a list, where the length of an empty list is zero and the length of a non-empty list is one plus the length of its tail.

List.set.code: List.set.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} : List α → ℕ → α → List α
List.set.comment:
`l.set n a` sets the value of list `l` at (zero-based) index `n` to `a`:
`[a, b, c, d].set 1 b' = [a, b', c, d]`
List.set.fullDefinition: def List.set : List α → Nat → α → List α   | cons _ as, 0,          b => cons b as   | cons a as, Nat.succ n, b => cons a (set as n b)   | nil,       _,          _ => nil
List.set.description: The operation updates a specified index of a list with a new element, replacing the existing value at that position.

Option.getD.code: Option.getD.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (opt : Option α) (dflt : α) : α
Option.getD.comment:
Get with default. If `opt : Option α` and `dflt : α`, then `opt.getD dflt`
returns `a` if `opt = some a` and `dflt` otherwise.

This function is `@[macro_inline]`, so `dflt` will not be evaluated unless
`opt` turns out to be `none`.
Option.getD.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def Option.getD (opt : Option α) (dflt : α) : α :=   match opt with   | some x => x   | none => dflt
Option.getD.description: This defines a function that retrieves a value from an optional type, returning a specified default value if the optional type is absent.

Nat.succ.comment:
The successor function on natural numbers, `succ n = n + 1`.
This is one of the two constructors of `Nat`. Using `succ n` should usually
be avoided in favor of `n + 1`, in order to remain compatible with the simp
normal form defined by `Nat.succ_eq_add_one`.
Nat.succ.description: This states the successor function for natural numbers, which yields the next integer by adding one to a given natural number.

List.get.code: List.get.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : Fin as.length → α
List.get.comment:
`as.get i` returns the `i`'th element of the list `as`.
This version of the function uses `i : Fin as.length` to ensure that it will
not index out of bounds.
List.get.fullDefinition: def List.get {α : Type u} : (as : List α) → Fin as.length → α   | cons a _,  ⟨0, _⟩ => a   | cons _ as, ⟨Nat.succ i, h⟩ => get as ⟨i, Nat.le_of_succ_le_succ h⟩
List.get.description: An indexed function retrieves the element at a specified position in a list, ensuring safety against out-of-bounds access.

ReaderT.code: ReaderT.{u, v} (ρ : Type u) (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type (max u v)
ReaderT.comment:
An implementation of Haskell's [`ReaderT`]. This is a monad transformer which
equips a monad with additional read-only state, of type `ρ`.

  [`ReaderT`]: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/transformers-0.5.5.0/docs/Control-Monad-Trans-Reader.html#t:ReaderT
ReaderT.fullDefinition: def ReaderT (ρ : Type u) (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type (max u v) :=   ρ → m α
ReaderT.description: This defines a monad transformer that adds read-only state functionality to an existing monad using a specified type.

Nat.pred.comment:
The predecessor function on natural numbers.

This definition is overridden in the compiler to use `n - 1` instead.
The definition provided here is the logical model.
Nat.pred.fullDefinition: def Nat.pred : (@& Nat) → Nat   | 0      => 0   | succ a => a
Nat.pred.description: The predecessor function for natural numbers returns the number that is one less than the given natural number.

Nat.zero_le.description: Zero is less than or equal to any natural number.

Pure.pure.code: Pure.pure.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : Pure f] {α : Type u} : α → f α
Pure.pure.comment:
If `a : α`, then `pure a : f α` represents a monadic action that does
nothing and returns `a`.
Pure.pure.fullDefinition: pure {α : Type u} : α → f α
Pure.pure.description: This defines a function that creates a monadic action that simply returns a given value without performing any additional computations.

ULift.up.code: ULift.up.{r, s} {α : Type s} (down : α) : ULift.{r, s} α
ULift.up.description: A value can be elevated into a specific type representing its lifted form.

Array.push.code: Array.push.{u} {α : Type u} (a : Array α) (v : α) : Array α
Array.push.comment:
Push an element onto the end of an array. This is amortized O(1) because
`Array α` is internally a dynamic array.
Array.push.fullDefinition: def Array.push {α : Type u} (a : Array α) (v : α) : Array α where   data := List.concat a.data v
Array.push.description: The operation adds an element to the end of an array, ensuring efficient performance by utilizing a dynamic array structure.

Functor.map.code: Functor.map.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : Functor f] {α β : Type u} : (α → β) → f α → f β
Functor.map.comment: If `f : α → β` and `x : F α` then `f <$> x : F β`.
Functor.map.fullDefinition: map : {α β : Type u} → (α → β) → f α → f β   /-- The special case `const a <$> x`, which can sometimes be implemented more   efficiently. -/   mapConst : {α β : Type u} → α → f β → f α := Function.comp map (Function.const _)
Functor.map.description: This defines a function that applies a mapping operation to a value wrapped in a context, transforming it from one type to another while preserving the structure of the context.

Neg.neg.code: Neg.neg.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Neg α] : α → α
Neg.neg.comment:
`-a` computes the negative or opposite of `a`.
The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
Neg.neg.description: This defines a function that calculates the negative or opposite value of a given element, depending on its type.

List.casesOn.code:
List.casesOn.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {motive : List α → Sort u_1} (t : List α) (nil : motive [])
  (cons : (head : α) → (tail : List α) → motive (head :: tail)) : motive t
List.casesOn.fullDefinition: inductive List (α : Type u) where   /-- `[]` is the empty list. -/   | nil : List α   /-- If `a : α` and `l : List α`, then `cons a l`, or `a :: l`, is the   list whose first element is `a` and with `l` as the rest of the list. -/   | cons (head : α) (tail : List α) : List α
List.casesOn.description: This defines a way to analyze a list by specifying different behaviors for the empty list and the case where the list has a head element and a tail.

inferInstance.comment:
`inferInstance` synthesizes a value of any target type by typeclass
inference. This function has the same type signature as the identity
function, but the square brackets on the `[i : α]` argument means that it will
attempt to construct this argument by typeclass inference. (This will fail if
`α` is not a `class`.) Example:
```
#check (inferInstance : Inhabited Nat) -- Inhabited Nat

def foo : Inhabited (Nat × Nat) :=
  inferInstance

example : foo.default = (default, default) :=
  rfl
```
inferInstance.fullDefinition: abbrev inferInstance {α : Sort u} [i : α] : α := i
inferInstance.description: This function generates an instance of a type by utilizing typeclass inference, acting like an identity function but specifically aiming to construct values required for class instances.

Char.ofNat.comment:
Convert a `Nat` into a `Char`. If the `Nat` does not encode a valid unicode scalar value,
`'\0'` is returned instead.
Char.ofNat.fullDefinition: def Char.ofNat (n : Nat) : Char :=   dite (n.isValidChar)     (fun h => Char.ofNatAux n h)     (fun _ => { val := ⟨{ val := 0, isLt := by decide }⟩, valid := Or.inl (by decide) })
Char.ofNat.description: This defines a function that converts a natural number into a character, returning a null character if the number does not represent a valid Unicode scalar value.

Prod.mk.code: Prod.mk.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (fst : α) (snd : β) : α × β
Prod.mk.comment: Constructs a pair from two terms.
Prod.mk.description: A pair is constructed from two given terms, resulting in a tuple that combines them.

Option.none.description: The construct represents the absence of a value in an option type, signifying that no valid data is present.

Dvd.dvd.code: Dvd.dvd.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [self : Dvd α] : α → α → Prop
Dvd.dvd.comment: Divisibility. `a ∣ b` (typed as `\|`) means that there is some `c` such that `b = a * c`.
Dvd.dvd.description: This defines a relation that indicates one element is a divisor of another in the context of a type that supports divisibility.

Eq.subst.code: Eq.subst.{u} {α : Sort u} {motive : α → Prop} {a b : α} (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : motive a) : motive b
Eq.subst.comment:
The substitution principle for equality. If `a = b ` and `P a` holds,
then `P b` also holds. We conventionally use the name `motive` for `P` here,
so that you can specify it explicitly using e.g.
`Eq.subst (motive := fun x => x < 5)` if it is not otherwise inferred correctly.

This theorem is the underlying mechanism behind the `rw` tactic, which is
essentially a fancy algorithm for finding good `motive` arguments to usefully
apply this theorem to replace occurrences of `a` with `b` in the goal or
hypotheses.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
Eq.subst.description: This theorem states that if two values are equal and a certain property holds for one of them, then it also holds for the other.

Or.elim.code: Or.elim {a b c : Prop} (h : a ∨ b) (left : a → c) (right : b → c) : c
Or.elim.comment:
Proof by cases on an `Or`. If `a ∨ b`, and both `a` and `b` imply
proposition `c`, then `c` is true.
Or.elim.description: This theorem establishes that if at least one of two propositions is true and both imply a third proposition, then the third proposition must also be true.

DecidableRel.code: DecidableRel.{u} {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)
DecidableRel.fullDefinition: abbrev DecidableRel {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) :=   (a b : α) → Decidable (r a b)
DecidableRel.description: This defines a type for relations on a set where it can be determined whether the relation holds between any two elements.

Append.append.code: Append.append.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Append α] : α → α → α
Append.append.comment: `a ++ b` is the result of concatenation of `a` and `b`. See `HAppend`.
Append.append.description: This defines a method for concatenating two elements of the same type into a single element, referred to as a concatenation operation.

cast.code: cast.{u} {α β : Sort u} (h : α = β) (a : α) : β
cast.comment:
Cast across a type equality. If `h : α = β` is an equality of types, and
`a : α`, then `a : β` will usually not typecheck directly, but this function
will allow you to work around this and embed `a` in type `β` as `cast h a : β`.

It is best to avoid this function if you can, because it is more complicated
to reason about terms containing casts, but if the types don't match up
definitionally sometimes there isn't anything better you can do.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
cast.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def cast {α β : Sort u} (h : Eq α β) (a : α) : β :=   h.rec a
cast.description: This defines a function that enables the conversion of a value from one type to another when given an equality proof between those types.

Seq.seq.code: Seq.seq.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : Seq f] {α β : Type u} : f (α → β) → (Unit → f α) → f β
Seq.seq.comment:
If `mf : F (α → β)` and `mx : F α`, then `mf <*> mx : F β`.
In a monad this is the same as `do let f ← mf; x ← mx; pure (f x)`:
it evaluates first the function, then the argument, and applies one to the other.

To avoid surprising evaluation semantics, `mx` is taken "lazily", using a
`Unit → f α` function.
Seq.seq.fullDefinition: seq : {α β : Type u} → f (α → β) → (Unit → f α) → f β
Seq.seq.description: This defines a function that combines a monadic function and a lazily evaluated argument to produce a result by applying the function to the argument.

LE.le.code: LE.le.{u} {α : Type u} [self : LE α] : α → α → Prop
LE.le.description: The less-equal relation establishes a comparison between two elements, indicating that the first element is less than or equal to the second.

Function.const.code: Function.const.{u, v} {α : Sort u} (β : Sort v) (a : α) : β → α
Function.const.comment:
The constant function. If `a : α`, then `Function.const β a : β → α` is the
"constant function with value `a`", that is, `Function.const β a b = a`.
```
example (b : Bool) : Function.const Bool 10 b = 10 :=
  rfl

#check Function.const Bool 10
-- Bool → Nat
```
Function.const.fullDefinition: @[inline] def Function.const {α : Sort u} (β : Sort v) (a : α) : β → α :=   fun _ => a
Function.const.description: This defines a constant function that, regardless of its input, always returns a specified fixed value.

And.intro.code: And.intro {a b : Prop} (left : a) (right : b) : a ∧ b
And.intro.comment: `And.intro : a → b → a ∧ b` is the constructor for the And operation.
And.intro.description: This states that if two propositions are true, then their conjunction is also true.

ULift.down.code: ULift.down.{r, s} {α : Type s} (self : ULift.{r, s} α) : α
ULift.down.fullDefinition: /-- Extract a value from `ULift α` -/ down : α
ULift.down.description: This function retrieves the original value from a lifted container that holds a value of a specified type.

Subtype.mk.code: Subtype.mk.{u} {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop} (val : α) (property : p val) : Subtype p
Subtype.mk.description: This theorem states that for any element and a property it satisfies, one can construct a subtype consisting of elements that possess that property.

Or.resolve_left.code: Or.resolve_left {a b : Prop} (h : a ∨ b) (na : ¬a) : b
Or.resolve_left.description: This theorem states that if one has a disjunction and knows that one of the propositions is false, then the other proposition must be true.

Bool.casesOn.code: Bool.casesOn.{u} {motive : Bool → Sort u} (t : Bool) (false : motive false) (true : motive true) : motive t
Bool.casesOn.fullDefinition: inductive Bool : Type where   /-- The boolean value `false`, not to be confused with the proposition `False`. -/   | false : Bool   /-- The boolean value `true`, not to be confused with the proposition `True`. -/   | true : Bool
Bool.casesOn.description: This defines a method to evaluate a boolean value by applying different outcomes based on whether it is true or false.

inferInstanceAs.comment:
`inferInstanceAs α` synthesizes a value of any target type by typeclass
inference. This is just like `inferInstance` except that `α` is given
explicitly instead of being inferred from the target type. It is especially
useful when the target type is some `α'` which is definitionally equal to `α`,
but the instance we are looking for is only registered for `α` (because
typeclass search does not unfold most definitions, but definitional equality
does.) Example:
```
#check inferInstanceAs (Inhabited Nat) -- Inhabited Nat
```
inferInstanceAs.fullDefinition: abbrev inferInstanceAs (α : Sort u) [i : α] : α := i
inferInstanceAs.description: This defines a function that explicitly synthesizes a value of a specific type using typeclass inference, which can be useful when the types involved are definitionally equal but the typeclass instance is only registered for one of them.

Nat.succ_le_succ.code: Nat.succ_le_succ {n m : ℕ} : n ≤ m → n.succ ≤ m.succ
Nat.succ_le_succ.description: If one natural number is less than or equal to another, then its successor is also less than or equal to the successor of the other number.

Fin.mk.code: Fin.mk {n : ℕ} (val : ℕ) (isLt : val < n) : Fin n
Fin.mk.comment: Creates a `Fin n` from `i : Nat` and a proof that `i < n`.
Fin.mk.description: This constructs a finite number type from a natural number along with a proof that the number is less than a specified limit.

Membership.mk.code: Membership.mk.{u, v} {α : outParam (Type u)} {γ : Type v} (mem : α → γ → Prop) : Membership α γ
Membership.mk.description: This constructs a membership relation that associates elements of one type with elements of another type through a specified property.

Unit.comment:
The unit type, the canonical type with one element, named `unit` or `()`.
In other words, it describes only a single value, which consists of said constructor applied
to no arguments whatsoever.
The `Unit` type is similar to `void` in languages derived from C.

`Unit` is actually defined as `PUnit.{1}` where `PUnit` is the universe
polymorphic version. The `Unit` should be preferred over `PUnit` where possible to avoid
unnecessary universe parameters.

In functional programming, `Unit` is the return type of things that "return
nothing", since a type with one element conveys no additional information.
When programming with monads, the type `m Unit` represents an action that has
some side effects but does not return a value, while `m α` would be an action
that has side effects and returns a value of type `α`.
Unit.description: This defines a type that contains exactly one value, used to indicate the absence of meaningful information.

MProd.mk.code: MProd.mk.{u} {α β : Type u} (fst : α) (snd : β) : MProd α β
MProd.mk.description: This constructs a product type using two elements from different types.

MonadLift.mk.code:
MonadLift.mk.{u, v, w} {m : semiOutParam (Type u → Type v)} {n : Type u → Type w}
  (monadLift : {α : Type u} → m α → n α) : MonadLift m n
MonadLift.mk.description: This theorem constructs a monad lifting mechanism that transforms operations from one monad into another through a specified lifting function.

ReaderT.run.code: ReaderT.run.{u, v} {ρ : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} {α : Type u} (x : ReaderT ρ m α) (r : ρ) : m α
ReaderT.run.comment:
If `x : ReaderT ρ m α` and `r : ρ`, then `x.run r : ρ` runs the monad with the
given reader state.
ReaderT.run.fullDefinition: def ReaderT.run {ρ : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} {α : Type u} (x : ReaderT ρ m α) (r : ρ) : m α :=   x r
ReaderT.run.description: The run function executes a reader monad with a specified environment, producing a result in the context of another monad.

True.intro.comment:
`True` is true, and `True.intro` (or more commonly, `trivial`)
is the proof.
True.intro.description: The statement establishes that the proposition of truth is inherently valid, with a specific proof confirming its truth.

And.left.code: And.left {a b : Prop} (self : a ∧ b) : a
And.left.comment:
Extract the left conjunct from a conjunction. `h : a ∧ b` then
`h.left`, also notated as `h.1`, is a proof of `a`.
And.left.description: From a conjunction of two propositions, it is possible to extract and prove the first proposition.

And.right.code: And.right {a b : Prop} (self : a ∧ b) : b
And.right.comment:
Extract the right conjunct from a conjunction. `h : a ∧ b` then
`h.right`, also notated as `h.2`, is a proof of `b`.
And.right.description: This theorem allows for the extraction of the second component from a conjunction when given a proof of that conjunction.

Option.some.code: Option.some.{u} {α : Type u} (val : α) : Option α
Option.some.description: This constructs an option type that encapsulates a value of a specified type.

Max.max.code: Max.max.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Max α] : α → α → α
Max.max.description: A function computes the maximum of two elements from a specified type.

not.comment:
`not x`, or `!x`, is the boolean "not" operation (not to be confused
with `Not : Prop → Prop`, which is the propositional connective).
not.fullDefinition: @[inline] def not : Bool → Bool   | true  => false   | false => true
not.description: The definition describes the boolean negation operation, which produces the opposite truth value of a given boolean input.

congrArg.code: congrArg.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {a₁ a₂ : α} (f : α → β) (h : a₁ = a₂) : f a₁ = f a₂
congrArg.comment:
Congruence in the function argument: if `a₁ = a₂` then `f a₁ = f a₂` for
any (nondependent) function `f`. This is more powerful than it might look at first, because
you can also use a lambda expression for `f` to prove that
`<something containing a₁> = <something containing a₂>`. This function is used
internally by tactics like `congr` and `simp` to apply equalities inside
subterms.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
congrArg.description: If two values are equal, then applying the same function to both yields equal results.

PUnit.unit.comment: `PUnit.unit : PUnit` is the canonical element of the unit type.
PUnit.unit.description: The unique element of the unit type is represented by a specific notation.

cond.code: cond.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Bool) (x y : α) : α
cond.comment:
`cond b x y` is the same as `if b then x else y`, but optimized for a
boolean condition. It can also be written as `bif b then x else y`.
This is `@[macro_inline]` because `x` and `y` should not
be eagerly evaluated (see `ite`).
cond.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def cond {α : Type u} (c : Bool) (x y : α) : α :=   match c with   | true  => x   | false => y
cond.description: This defines a conditional expression that evaluates to one of two values based on a boolean condition, optimized for efficiency.

Min.min.code: Min.min.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Min α] : α → α → α
Min.min.description: This defines a minimum operation that takes two elements and returns the lesser of the two.

Sub.sub.code: Sub.sub.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Sub α] : α → α → α
Sub.sub.comment: `a - b` computes the difference of `a` and `b`. See `HSub`.
Sub.sub.description: This defines an operation that calculates the difference between two elements in a given type.

Option.map.code: Option.map.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β) : Option α → Option β
Option.map.comment:
Map a function over an `Option` by applying the function to the contained
value if present.
Option.map.fullDefinition: @[inline] protected def Option.map (f : α → β) : Option α → Option β   | some x => some (f x)   | none   => none
Option.map.description: This defines a function that applies a given transformation to the value inside an optional type if it is present, resulting in a new optional type.

Nat.casesOn.code: Nat.casesOn.{u} {motive : ℕ → Sort u} (t : ℕ) (zero : motive zero) (succ : (n : ℕ) → motive n.succ) : motive t
Nat.casesOn.fullDefinition: inductive Nat where   /-- `Nat.zero`, is the smallest natural number. This is one of the two   constructors of `Nat`. Using `Nat.zero` should usually be avoided in favor of   `0 : Nat` or simply `0`, in order to remain compatible with the simp normal   form defined by `Nat.zero_eq`. -/   | zero : Nat   /-- The successor function on natural numbers, `succ n = n + 1`.   This is one of the two constructors of `Nat`. Using `succ n` should usually   be avoided in favor of `n + 1`, in order to remain compatible with the simp   normal form defined by `Nat.succ_eq_add_one`. -/   | succ (n : Nat) : Nat
Nat.casesOn.description: This defines a method to evaluate a natural number by applying different outcomes based on whether it is zero or a successor of a number.

Option.casesOn.code:
Option.casesOn.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {motive : Option α → Sort u_1} (t : Option α) (none : motive none)
  (some : (val : α) → motive (some val)) : motive t
Option.casesOn.fullDefinition: inductive Option (α : Type u) where   /-- No value. -/   | none : Option α   /-- Some value of type `α`. -/   | some (val : α) : Option α
Option.casesOn.description: This defines a mechanism for performing case analysis on an optional value, allowing the application of different rules based on whether the value is present or absent.

Nat.zero.comment:
`Nat.zero`, is the smallest natural number. This is one of the two
constructors of `Nat`. Using `Nat.zero` should usually be avoided in favor of
`0 : Nat` or simply `0`, in order to remain compatible with the simp normal
form defined by `Nat.zero_eq`.
Nat.zero.description: This theorem identifies the smallest natural number as zero, which serves as a constructor for natural numbers.

Option.recOn.code:
Option.recOn.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {motive : Option α → Sort u_1} (t : Option α) (none : motive none)
  (some : (val : α) → motive (some val)) : motive t
Option.recOn.fullDefinition: inductive Option (α : Type u) where   /-- No value. -/   | none : Option α   /-- Some value of type `α`. -/   | some (val : α) : Option α
Option.recOn.description: This defines a function that allows for pattern matching on an optional value, applying different motives based on whether the value is present or absent.

Unit.unit.comment:
`Unit.unit : Unit` is the canonical element of the unit type.
It can also be written as `()`.
Unit.unit.description: This defines a unique element of the unit type, which is a type that has only one possible value.

Bind.bind.code: Bind.bind.{u, v} {m : Type u → Type v} [self : Bind m] {α β : Type u} : m α → (α → m β) → m β
Bind.bind.comment:
If `x : m α` and `f : α → m β`, then `x >>= f : m β` represents the
result of executing `x` to get a value of type `α` and then passing it to `f`.
Bind.bind.fullDefinition: bind : {α β : Type u} → m α → (α → m β) → m β
Bind.bind.description: This defines a function that executes a computation within a monadic context to obtain a result and then applies a function to that result, producing a new computation in the same context.

Add.add.code: Add.add.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Add α] : α → α → α
Add.add.comment: `a + b` computes the sum of `a` and `b`. See `HAdd`.
Add.add.description: This defines a function that computes the sum of two elements of a type that supports addition.

Div.mk.code: Div.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (div : α → α → α) : Div α
Div.mk.description: This construct defines a method for creating a division structure that specifies how to divide elements of a particular type.

Pow.mk.code: Pow.mk.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (pow : α → β → α) : Pow α β
Pow.mk.description: This theorem constructs a power type using a function that combines elements from one type with those from another.

Mul.mk.code: Mul.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (mul : α → α → α) : Mul α
Mul.mk.description: This theorem asserts that for any type and a binary multiplication operation defined on that type, one can create a structured object representing the multiplicative properties of that type.

Bool.recOn.code: Bool.recOn.{u} {motive : Bool → Sort u} (t : Bool) (false : motive false) (true : motive true) : motive t
Bool.recOn.fullDefinition: inductive Bool : Type where   /-- The boolean value `false`, not to be confused with the proposition `False`. -/   | false : Bool   /-- The boolean value `true`, not to be confused with the proposition `True`. -/   | true : Bool
Bool.recOn.description: This defines a function that allows for recursion on the Boolean type, providing a way to derive a result based on its value of either true or false.

Nonempty.elim.code: Nonempty.elim.{u} {α : Sort u} {p : Prop} (h₁ : Nonempty α) (h₂ : α → p) : p
Nonempty.elim.comment:
The elimination principle for `Nonempty α`. If `Nonempty α`, and we can
prove `p` given any element `x : α`, then `p` holds. Note that it is essential
that `p` is a `Prop` here; the version with `p` being a `Sort u` is equivalent
to `Classical.choice`.
Nonempty.elim.description: If a type is non-empty and we can derive a proposition from any element of that type, then the proposition is true.

Eq.ndrec.code: Eq.ndrec.{u1, u2} {α : Sort u2} {a : α} {motive : α → Sort u1} (m : motive a) {b : α} (h : a = b) : motive b
Eq.ndrec.comment: Non-dependent recursor for the equality type.
Eq.ndrec.fullDefinition: inductive Eq : α → α → Prop where   /-- `Eq.refl a : a = a` is reflexivity, the unique constructor of the   equality type. See also `rfl`, which is usually used instead. -/   | refl (a : α) : Eq a a
Eq.ndrec.description: This defines a method to derive properties of a given type from a specific instance of equality, allowing transitions between equal values while preserving a specified motive.

Fin.val.comment:
If `i : Fin n`, then `i.val : ℕ` is the described number. It can also be
written as `i.1` or just `i` when the target type is known.
Fin.val.fullDefinition: val  : Nat   /-- If `i : Fin n`, then `i.2` is a proof that `i.1 < n`. -/   isLt : LT.lt val n
Fin.val.description: This defines how to extract the natural number represented by a finite index.

Subtype.property.code: Subtype.property.{u} {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop} (self : Subtype p) : p ↑self
Subtype.property.comment:
If `s : {x // p x}` then `s.2` or `s.property` is the assertion that
`p s.1`, that is, that `s` is in fact an element for which `p` holds.
Subtype.property.description: This theorem states that for any element of a subtype defined by a property, that element satisfies the property itself.

Add.mk.code: Add.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (add : α → α → α) : Add α
Add.mk.description: This establishes a method to create an addition structure for a type by providing a binary operation that combines two elements of that type.

Neg.mk.code: Neg.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (neg : α → α) : Neg α
Neg.mk.description: This theorem constructs a negation instance for a type by providing a specific negation function.

Sub.mk.code: Sub.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (sub : α → α → α) : Sub α
Sub.mk.description: This theorem describes the construction of a subset from a given set using a specified binary operation on its elements.

eq_of_heq.code: eq_of_heq.{u} {α : Sort u} {a a' : α} (h : HEq a a') : a = a'
eq_of_heq.description: This theorem establishes that if two elements are judged to be equal in a higher equality context, they are also equal in the standard sense of equality.

List.recOn.code:
List.recOn.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {motive : List α → Sort u_1} (t : List α) (nil : motive [])
  (cons : (head : α) → (tail : List α) → motive tail → motive (head :: tail)) : motive t
List.recOn.fullDefinition: inductive List (α : Type u) where   /-- `[]` is the empty list. -/   | nil : List α   /-- If `a : α` and `l : List α`, then `cons a l`, or `a :: l`, is the   list whose first element is `a` and with `l` as the rest of the list. -/   | cons (head : α) (tail : List α) : List α
List.recOn.description: This defines a recursion principle for lists that allows the development of properties or functions based on their structure, starting with the empty list and building from the head and tail of non-empty lists.

List.noConfusion.code: List.noConfusion.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {P : Sort u_1} {v1 v2 : List α} (h12 : v1 = v2) : List.noConfusionType P v1 v2
List.noConfusion.fullDefinition: inductive List (α : Type u) where   /-- `[]` is the empty list. -/   | nil : List α   /-- If `a : α` and `l : List α`, then `cons a l`, or `a :: l`, is the   list whose first element is `a` and with `l` as the rest of the list. -/   | cons (head : α) (tail : List α) : List α
List.noConfusion.description: This defines a principle that allows reasoning about two equal lists by eliminating confusion between them when a proof of their equality is provided.

absurd.code: absurd.{v} {a : Prop} {b : Sort v} (h₁ : a) (h₂ : ¬a) : b
absurd.comment:
Anything follows from two contradictory hypotheses. Example:
```
example (hp : p) (hnp : ¬p) : q := absurd hp hnp
```
For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
absurd.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def absurd {a : Prop} {b : Sort v} (h₁ : a) (h₂ : Not a) : b :=   (h₂ h₁).rec
absurd.description: This establishes a principle that allows one to derive any statement from a proposition and its negation, highlighting the nature of contradictions in logic.

String.mk.comment:
Pack a `List Char` into a `String`. This function is overridden by the
compiler and is O(n) in the length of the list.
String.mk.description: This theorem defines a method to encapsulate a list of characters into a string format, ensuring efficient conversion based on the list's length.

LT.lt.code: LT.lt.{u} {α : Type u} [self : LT α] : α → α → Prop
LT.lt.description: This defines a less-than relation for elements of a given type, indicating a way to compare their order.

Nat.not_succ_le_self.description: The theorem states that the successor of a natural number is never less than or equal to the original number itself.

Fin.val_eq_of_eq.code: Fin.val_eq_of_eq {n : ℕ} {i j : Fin n} (h : i = j) : ↑i = ↑j
Fin.val_eq_of_eq.description: This theorem asserts that if two finite numbers are equal, their corresponding values as natural numbers are also equal.

LT.mk.code: LT.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (lt : α → α → Prop) : LT α
LT.mk.description: This theorem constructs a linear order from a binary relation that defines which elements are less than others.

LE.mk.code: LE.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (le : α → α → Prop) : LE α
LE.mk.description: This establishes a constructor for a linear order structure that takes a binary relation defining the ordering on a type.

Eq.recOn.code:
Eq.recOn.{u, u_1} {α : Sort u_1} :
  {a : α} → {motive : (a_1 : α) → a = a_1 → Sort u} → {a_1 : α} → (t : a = a_1) → motive a ⋯ → motive a_1 t
Eq.recOn.fullDefinition: inductive Eq : α → α → Prop where   /-- `Eq.refl a : a = a` is reflexivity, the unique constructor of the   equality type. See also `rfl`, which is usually used instead. -/   | refl (a : α) : Eq a a
Eq.recOn.description: This defines a function that allows reasoning about equality by recursing on an equality proof, enabling the application of a specified motive to both sides of the equality.

Decidable.decide.comment:
Convert a decidable proposition into a boolean value.

If `p : Prop` is decidable, then `decide p : Bool` is the boolean value
which is `true` if `p` is true and `false` if `p` is false.
Decidable.decide.fullDefinition: @[inline_if_reduce, nospecialize] def Decidable.decide (p : Prop) [h : Decidable p] : Bool :=   h.casesOn (fun _ => false) (fun _ => true)
Decidable.decide.description: This defines a function that converts a decidable proposition into a boolean value indicating its truth or falsehood.

Fin.eq_of_val_eq.code: Fin.eq_of_val_eq {n : ℕ} {i j : Fin n} : ↑i = ↑j → i = j
Fin.eq_of_val_eq.description: This theorem states that if two finite numbers are equal when viewed as natural numbers, then they are equal as finite numbers as well.

Mul.mul.code: Mul.mul.{u} {α : Type u} [self : Mul α] : α → α → α
Mul.mul.comment: `a * b` computes the product of `a` and `b`. See `HMul`.
Mul.mul.description: This defines a binary operation that calculates the product of two elements in a type that supports multiplication.

OfNat.ofNat.code: OfNat.ofNat.{u} {α : Type u} : (x : ℕ) → [self : OfNat α x] → α
OfNat.ofNat.comment:
The `OfNat.ofNat` function is automatically inserted by the parser when
the user writes a numeric literal like `1 : α`. Implementations of this
typeclass can therefore customize the behavior of `n : α` based on `n` and
`α`.
OfNat.ofNat.description: This defines a function that converts a natural number into a type defined by the OfNat typeclass, allowing customization of numeric literals based on their type.

congr.code: congr.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {f₁ f₂ : α → β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h₁ : f₁ = f₂) (h₂ : a₁ = a₂) : f₁ a₁ = f₂ a₂
congr.comment:
Congruence in both function and argument. If `f₁ = f₂` and `a₁ = a₂` then
`f₁ a₁ = f₂ a₂`. This only works for nondependent functions; the theorem
statement is more complex in the dependent case.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
congr.description: This theorem asserts that if two functions are equal and their corresponding arguments are equal, then applying these functions to these arguments will yield equal results.

Lean.ParserDescr.symbol.comment:
A literal symbol parser: parses `val` as a literal.
This parser does not work on identifiers, so `symbol` arguments are declared
as "keywords" and cannot be used as identifiers anywhere in the file.
Lean.ParserDescr.symbol.description: This theorem defines a parser that interprets a specified string as a literal symbol, which cannot be used as an identifier within the file.

dite.code: dite.{u} {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t : c → α) (e : ¬c → α) : α
dite.comment:
"Dependent" if-then-else, normally written via the notation `if h : c then t(h) else e(h)`,
is sugar for `dite c (fun h => t(h)) (fun h => e(h))`, and it is the same as
`if c then t else e` except that `t` is allowed to depend on a proof `h : c`,
and `e` can depend on `h : ¬c`. (Both branches use the same name for the hypothesis,
even though it has different types in the two cases.)

We use this to be able to communicate the if-then-else condition to the branches.
For example, `Array.get arr ⟨i, h⟩` expects a proof `h : i < arr.size` in order to
avoid a bounds check, so you can write `if h : i < arr.size then arr.get ⟨i, h⟩ else ...`
to avoid the bounds check inside the if branch. (Of course in this case we have only
lifted the check into an explicit `if`, but we could also use this proof multiple times
or derive `i < arr.size` from some other proposition that we are checking in the `if`.)
dite.fullDefinition: @[macro_inline] def dite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t : c → α) (e : Not c → α) : α :=   h.casesOn e t
dite.description: This defines a dependent if-then-else mechanism that allows for conditional branching based on a proposition, where the outcome can depend on proofs of both the truth and falsehood of that proposition.

Trans.mk.code:
Trans.mk.{u, v, w, u_1, u_2, u_3} {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2} {γ : Sort u_3} {r : α → β → Sort u} {s : β → γ → Sort v}

Trans.mk.description: This theorem establishes a framework for defining a transitive relation connecting two binary relations, allowing one to infer a relationship between elements of a first and third type through an intermediary relationship.

Trans.trans.comment: Compose two proofs by transitivity, generalized over the relations involved.
Trans.trans.fullDefinition: trans : r a b → s b c → t a c
Trans.trans.description: This defines a method to combine two relationships into a new relationship using transitivity, applicable across various types and relations.

Classical.ofNonempty.comment:

congrFun.code: congrFun.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} {f g : (x : α) → β x} (h : f = g) (a : α) : f a = g a
congrFun.comment: Congruence in the function part of an application: If `f = g` then `f a = g a`.

Pure.mk.code: Pure.mk.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} (pure : {α : Type u} → α → f α) : Pure f
Pure.mk.description: This establishes a constructor that wraps a function into a pure context, enabling computations in a structured way.

Bind.mk.code: Bind.mk.{u, v} {m : Type u → Type v} (bind : {α β : Type u} → m α → (α → m β) → m β) : Bind m
Bind.mk.description: This describes the construction of a binding operation for a type constructor that allows chaining of computations in a monadic context.

Lean.Syntax.ident.code:
Lean.Syntax.ident (info : Lean.SourceInfo) (rawVal : Substring) (val : Lean.Name)

Lean.Syntax.ident.comment:
An `ident` corresponds to an identifier as parsed by the `ident` or

modify.code: modify.{u, v} {σ : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} [MonadState σ m] (f : σ → σ) : m PUnit.{u + 1}
modify.comment:
`modify (f : σ → σ)` applies the function `f` to the state.

It is equivalent to `do set (f (← get))`, but `modify f` may be preferable
because the former does not use the state linearly (without sufficient inlining).
modify.fullDefinition: def modify {σ : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} [MonadState σ m] (f : σ → σ) : m PUnit :=   modifyGet fun s => (PUnit.unit, f s)
modify.description: This defines a function that updates the state in a monadic context by applying a given function to the current state.

PLift.down.code: PLift.down.{u} {α : Sort u} (self : PLift α) : α
PLift.down.fullDefinition: /-- Extract a value from `PLift α` -/ down : α
PLift.down.description: This defines a function that retrieves the underlying value from a lifted type, effectively reversing the lifting process.

SeqLeft.seqLeft.code: SeqLeft.seqLeft.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : SeqLeft f] {α β : Type u} : f α → (Unit → f β) → f α
SeqLeft.seqLeft.comment:
If `x : F α` and `y : F β`, then `x <* y` evaluates `x`, then `y`,
and returns the result of `x`.

To avoid surprising evaluation semantics, `y` is taken "lazily", using a
`Unit → f β` function.
SeqLeft.seqLeft.fullDefinition: seqLeft : {α β : Type u} → f α → (Unit → f β) → f α
SeqLeft.seqLeft.description: This defines a function that takes a value and a lazily evaluated function, performing an operation that first evaluates the initial value and then applies the second function, returning the result of the first evaluation.

SeqRight.seqRight.code: SeqRight.seqRight.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : SeqRight f] {α β : Type u} : f α → (Unit → f β) → f β
SeqRight.seqRight.comment:
If `x : F α` and `y : F β`, then `x *> y` evaluates `x`, then `y`,
and returns the result of `y`.

To avoid surprising evaluation semantics, `y` is taken "lazily", using a
`Unit → f β` function.
SeqRight.seqRight.fullDefinition: seqRight : {α β : Type u} → f α → (Unit → f β) → f β
SeqRight.seqRight.description: This defines a function that combines two computations, where the second computation is executed lazily after the first one has completed.

Functor.mapConst.code: Functor.mapConst.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [self : Functor f] {α β : Type u} : α → f β → f α
Functor.mapConst.comment:
The special case `const a <$> x`, which can sometimes be implemented more
efficiently.
Functor.mapConst.fullDefinition: mapConst : {α β : Type u} → α → f β → f α := Function.comp map (Function.const _)
Functor.mapConst.description: This defines a function that applies a constant value to a functorial context, transforming an inner structure while preserving the outer one.

Lean.MacroM.comment:
The `MacroM` monad is the main monad for macro expansion. It has the
information needed to handle hygienic name generation, and is the monad that
`macro` definitions live in.

Notably, this is a (relatively) pure monad: there is no `IO` and no access to
the `Environment`. That means that things like declaration lookup are
impossible here, as well as `IO.Ref` or other side-effecting operations.
For more capabilities, macros can instead be written as `elab` using `adaptExpander`.
Lean.MacroM.fullDefinition: abbrev MacroM := ReaderT Macro.Context (EStateM Macro.Exception Macro.State)
Lean.MacroM.description: This defines a monad used for macro expansion that manages name generation while remaining purely functional without access to side effects or environment lookups.

Lean.withRef.code: Lean.withRef {m : Type → Type} [Monad m] [MonadRef m] {α : Type} (ref : Syntax) (x : m α) : m α
Lean.withRef.comment:
Run `x : m α` with a modified value for the `ref`. This is not exactly
the same as `MonadRef.withRef`, because it uses `replaceRef` to avoid putting
syntax with bad spans in the state.
Lean.withRef.fullDefinition: def withRef [Monad m] [MonadRef m] {α} (ref : Syntax) (x : m α) : m α :=   bind getRef fun oldRef =>   let ref := replaceRef ref oldRef   MonadRef.withRef ref x
Lean.withRef.description: This defines a method to execute a monadic computation with a temporarily altered reference value while ensuring the original context remains valid.

Using `Nat.zero` should usually be avoided in favor of   `0 : Nat` or simply `0`, in order to remain compatible with the simp normal   form defined by `Nat.zero_eq`. -/   | zero : Nat   /-- The successor function on natural numbers, `succ n = n + 1`.   This is one of the two constructors of `Nat`. Using `succ n` should usually   be avoided in favor of `n + 1`, in order to remain compatible with the simp   normal form defined by `Nat.succ_eq_add_one`. -/   | succ (n : Nat) : Nat
Nat.recOn.description: This function defines a way to construct a proof or value for a specified type based on an initial case for zero and a rule for how to handle successor cases in the natural numbers.

semiOutParam.comment:
Gadget for marking semi output parameters in type classes.

Semi-output parameters influence the order in which arguments to type class
instances are processed.  Lean determines an order where all non-(semi-)output
parameters to the instance argument have to be figured out before attempting to
synthesize an argument (that is, they do not contain assignable metavariables
created during TC synthesis). This rules out instances such as `[Mul β] : Add
α` (because `β` could be anything). Marking a parameter as semi-output is a
promise that instances of the type class will always fill in a value for that
parameter.

For example, the `Coe` class is defined as:
```
class Coe (α : semiOutParam (Sort u)) (β : Sort v)
```
This means that all `Coe` instances should provide a concrete value for `α`
(i.e., not an assignable metavariable). An instance like `Coe Nat Int` or `Coe
α (Option α)` is fine, but `Coe α Nat` is not since it does not provide a value
for `α`.
semiOutParam.fullDefinition: @[reducible] def semiOutParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α
semiOutParam.description: This defines a type of parameter that influences how type class instances are processed, ensuring that certain parameters are treated as semi-output and always receive concrete values during instance synthesis.

Or.intro_left.code: Or.intro_left {a : Prop} (b : Prop) (h : a) : a ∨ b
Or.intro_left.description: This theorem provides a way to conclude that if a proposition is true, then that proposition implies the disjunction of itself and any other proposition.

optParam.code: optParam.{u} (α : Sort u) (default : α) : Sort u
optParam.comment:
Gadget for optional parameter support.

A binder like `(x : α := default)` in a declaration is syntax sugar for
`x : optParam α default`, and triggers the elaborator to attempt to use
`default` to supply the argument if it is not supplied.
optParam.fullDefinition: @[reducible] def optParam (α : Sort u) (default : α) : Sort u := α
optParam.description: This defines a mechanism for creating optional parameters in declarations, allowing a default value to be used if no value is provided.

Or.recOn.code:
Or.recOn {a b : Prop} {motive : a ∨ b → Prop} (t : a ∨ b) (inl : ∀ (h : a), motive ⋯) (inr : ∀ (h : b), motive ⋯) :
  motive t
Or.recOn.fullDefinition: inductive Or (a b : Prop) : Prop where   /-- `Or.inl` is "left injection" into an `Or`. If `h : a` then `Or.inl h : a ∨ b`. -/   | inl (h : a) : Or a b   /-- `Or.inr` is "right injection" into an `Or`. If `h : b` then `Or.inr h : a ∨ b`. -/   | inr (h : b) : Or a b
Or.recOn.description: This defines a function that allows one to reason about propositions in a disjunction by providing different cases for each possible truth value.

Lean.Name.anonymous.description: This theorem defines a representation for an anonymous name in a naming system.

Lean.Name.str.comment:

Lean.Name.num.comment:
A numerical name. This kind of name is used, for example, to create hierarchical names for
free variables and metavariables. The identifier `_uniq.231` is represented as
```lean
.num (.str .anonymous "_uniq") 231
```
Lean.Name.num.description: This describes a method for creating a numerical name, which can be utilized to form hierarchical names for free variables and metavariables.

Char.utf8Size.description: This defines a function that determines the byte size needed to represent a character in the UTF-8 encoding.

Lean.SourceInfo.original.code:
Lean.SourceInfo.original (leading : Substring) (pos : String.Pos) (trailing : Substring) (endPos : String.Pos) :
  SourceInfo
Lean.SourceInfo.original.comment:
Token from original input with whitespace and position information.
`leading` will be inferred after parsing by `Syntax.updateLeading`. During parsing,
it is not at all clear what the preceding token was, especially with backtracking.
Lean.SourceInfo.original.description: This theorem describes a structure that encapsulates information about a source token, including its surrounding whitespace and positional details within the original input.

Lean.SourceInfo.synthetic.code: Lean.SourceInfo.synthetic (pos endPos : String.Pos) (canonical : Bool := false) : SourceInfo
Lean.SourceInfo.synthetic.comment:
Synthesized syntax (e.g. from a quotation) annotated with a span from the original source.
In the delaborator, we "misuse" this constructor to store synthetic positions identifying
subterms.

The `canonical` flag on synthetic syntax is enabled for syntax that is not literally part
of the original input syntax but should be treated "as if" the user really wrote it
for the purpose of hovers and error messages. This is usually used on identifiers,
to connect the binding site to the user's original syntax even if the name of the identifier
changes during expansion, as well as on tokens where we will attach targeted messages.

The syntax `token%$stx` in a syntax quotation will annotate the token `token` with the span
from `stx` and also mark it as canonical.

As a rough guide, a macro expansion should only use a given piece of input syntax in
a single canonical token, although this is sometimes violated when the same identifier
is used to declare two binders, as in the macro expansion for dependent if:
```
`(if $h : $cond then $t else $e) ~>
`(dite $cond (fun $h => $t) (fun $h => $t))
```
In these cases if the user hovers over `h` they will see information about both binding sites.
Lean.SourceInfo.synthetic.description: This theorem creates synthesized syntax information that spans a specified position in the original source, optionally denoting it as canonical for better user feedback in error messages and hover tips.

Lean.SourceInfo.none.description: This states that there is a token representing a source information object that lacks any positioning details.

Lean.Syntax.node.code: Lean.Syntax.node (info : SourceInfo) (kind : SyntaxNodeKind) (args : Array Syntax) : Syntax
Lean.Syntax.node.comment:
Node in the syntax tree.

The `info` field is used by the delaborator to store the position of the
subexpression corresponding to this node. The parser sets the `info` field
to `none`.
The parser sets the `info` field to `none`, with position retrieval continuing recursively.
Nodes created by quotations use the result from `SourceInfo.fromRef` so that they are marked
as synthetic even when the leading/trailing token is not.
The delaborator uses the `info` field to store the position of the subexpression
corresponding to this node.

(Remark: the `node` constructor did not have an `info` field in previous
versions. This caused a bug in the interactive widgets, where the popup for
`a + b` was the same as for `a`. The delaborator used to associate
subexpressions with pretty-printed syntax by setting the (string) position
of the first atom/identifier to the (expression) position of the
subexpression. For example, both `a` and `a + b` have the same first
identifier, and so their infos got mixed up.)
Lean.Syntax.node.description: This defines a structure representing a node in a syntax tree, which includes information about its source position and type, facilitating accurate representation and parsing of expressions.

Lean.SyntaxNodeKind.comment:
A `SyntaxNodeKind` classifies `Syntax.node` values. It is an abbreviation for
`Name`, and you can use name literals to construct `SyntaxNodeKind`s, but
they need not refer to declarations in the environment. Conventionally, a
`SyntaxNodeKind` will correspond to the `Parser` or `ParserDesc` declaration
that parses it.
Lean.SyntaxNodeKind.description: This defines a type that categorizes syntax nodes in a programming environment.

MonadState.modifyGet.code:
MonadState.modifyGet.{u, v} {σ : outParam (Type u)} {m : Type u → Type v} [self : MonadState σ m] {α : Type u} :
  (σ → α × σ) → m α
MonadState.modifyGet.comment:
`modifyGet (f : σ → α × σ)` applies `f` to the current state, replaces
the state with the return value, and returns a computed value.

It is equivalent to `do let (a, s) := f (← get); put s; pure a`, but
`modifyGet f` may be preferable because the former does not use the state
linearly (without sufficient inlining).
MonadState.modifyGet.fullDefinition: modifyGet {α : Type u} : (σ → Prod α σ) → m α
MonadState.modifyGet.description: This function allows for modifying the state by applying a transformation to it, updating the state accordingly, and simultaneously returning a computed value derived from the original state.

unsafeCast.code: unsafeCast.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (a : α) : β
unsafeCast.comment:
This function will cast a value of type `α` to type `β`, and is a no-op in the
compiler. This function is **extremely dangerous** because there is no guarantee
that types `α` and `β` have the same data representation, and this can lead to
memory unsafety. It is also logically unsound, since you could just cast
`True` to `False`. For all those reasons this function is marked as `unsafe`.

It is implemented by lifting both `α` and `β` into a common universe, and then
using `cast (lcProof : ULift (PLift α) = ULift (PLift β))` to actually perform
the cast. All these operations are no-ops in the compiler.

Using this function correctly requires some knowledge of the data representation
of the source and target types. Some general classes of casts which are safe in
the current runtime:

* `Array α` to `Array β` where `α` and `β` have compatible representations,
  or more generally for other inductive types.
* `Quot α r` and `α`.
* `@Subtype α p` and `α`, or generally any structure containing only one
  non-`Prop` field of type `α`.
* Casting `α` to/from `NonScalar` when `α` is a boxed generic type
  (i.e. a function that accepts an arbitrary type `α` and is not specialized to
  a scalar type like `UInt8`).
unsafeCast.fullDefinition: unsafe def unsafeCast {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (a : α) : β :=   PLift.down (ULift.down.{max u v} (cast lcProof (ULift.up.{max u v} (PLift.up a))))
unsafeCast.description: This defines a function that forcibly and unsafely converts a value from one type to another without any guarantees about the compatibility of those types, posing significant risks for memory safety and logical consistency.

Not.comment:
`Not p`, or `¬p`, is the negation of `p`. It is defined to be `p → False`,
so if your goal is `¬p` you can use `intro h` to turn the goal into
`h : p ⊢ False`, and if you have `hn : ¬p` and `h : p` then `hn h : False`
and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.
For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
Not.fullDefinition: def Not (a : Prop) : Prop := a → False
Not.description: This defines the concept of negation in propositional logic as the implication that asserting a proposition leads to a contradiction.

PLift.up.code: PLift.up.{u} {α : Sort u} (down : α) : PLift α
PLift.up.description: This theorem demonstrates the process of placing a value from its original type into a specific lifted structure that represents that type.
